newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia October c/a data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia October c/a data.

text.p: Australia's seasonally adjusted current account deficit came in at A$1.788 billion in October, compared with median forecasts for a A$1.60 billion deficit.
Estimates for October had ranged from A$1.5 to A$1.95 billion after the September deficit of A$1.69 billion.
The following is a selection of economists' initial reactions to the data.
TIM PFITZNER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"It's certainly not trade balance effect. That was pretty much as it was last month. It seems to be all on the income side and I wouldn't expect it to be moving our expectations about interest rates at this stage."

"It's broadly in line with expectations. Exports were up a fraction which is pleasing. The big concern is the net income deficit which widened. Over time, the government's fiscal policy aimed at improving national savings should lead to a better trend on the current account. But again those fiscal tightenings are coming through over a number of years and any improvement on the bottom line current account will be several years away, at least in the structural sense. There is certainly no implications for interest rates."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It's worrying that we still have such a wide income deficit at a time when global interest rates are low. The structure of the macro-economy is pretty good, but it's the poor savings, that we have heard about for over a decade now, are still relevent. The ground swell of people suggesting that we need to do something about national savings is only translating very, very slowly into action on the political scene."
KAREN PRINGLE, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ

"On the trade side, it's roughly as we were expecting. It is disappointing to see the further deterioration in the net income component. However, the deficit is not rising by enough to have the market concerned. So long as the current account is running at below A$2 billion a month, I think the market will probably be comfortable with this."
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP INVESTMENTS

"The trade balance has come in slightly better than we'd expected, while the net income deficit has come in slightly worse. Overall, then, we don't see the result as much of a surprise. But it does serve as a reminder that the current account deficit is still a problem. And all we've really seen to date is a normal cyclical improvement."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It was a bit higher than we were thinking. We were looking for more of a rebound than we actually saw, although the weakness, which was all in the rural side, wasn't all that surprising given what's happened to key commodity prices such as wheat over the past month or two. The net income deficit turned out to be a bit higher. It's still very large and likely to remain large for a long time and while it does you have a higher floor under the current account deficit. It will be very difficult to sustain the lower numbers we saw a few months ago. You would have to expect that if activity is going to pick up over the next year that there will be a widening of the deficit."
